newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: U.N. draws up corruption action plan in Argentina.
newsitem.headline: U.N. draws up corruption action plan in Argentina.

text.p: A United Nations panel of anti-corruption experts began a week of talks in Argentina on Monday to draw up a plan of action to include a practical manual and a "model" law to help governments combat graft.

The 10 experts summoned to brainstorm recommendations against the spread of corruption for U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan include former U.S. Attorney General Dick Thornburgh and the Russian Accounts Tribunal chief Fyodor Shelyuto.

"In the face of the globalization of crime we have to find effective instruments to fight organised crime and one of its typical activities -- corruption," said Argentine Justice Minister Elias Jassan, inaugurating the closed-door talks.

But Jassan, vice-president of the U.N. Committee on Crime Prevention and Penal Justice, was grilled by reporters about Argentina's credibility to host such talks when the Peronist government itself has a poor reputation on graft.

Jassan and Interior Minister Carlos Corach have been named by former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo as chief manipulators of the Argentine courts to protect businessmen involved in graft and tax evasion. They both deny the charges and are taking legal action against Cavallo.
Jassan denied there was any link between allegedly high levels of corruption in Argentina, a common complaint among foreign investors, and the U.N. talks.

"It shows our government's commitment in the fight against corruption," said Jassan, repeating the government line that wholesale privatisation since President Carlos Menem came to power in 1989 has "dismantled existing structures" for graft.

In his opening speech, Jassan said: "Corruption in its different forms hurts countries by destabilising institutions, altering the rules of competition, creating unease in society and mistrust in the institutions of the republic."

In Argentina, corruption at high levels has been on the front pages of newspapers for weeks, with a federal judge caught dealing with smugglers by television cameras and Menem questioned over the funding of an airstrip and country houses in his native desert province of La Rioja.

But the chairman of the Buenos Aires talks, Eugenio Maria Curia, head of international affairs at the Argentine Justice Ministry, said his country was fighting graft with mechanisms such as a new Public Ethics Office "to close our defences so that there can be no impunity for cases of bribery and corruption that might exist."

Curia said his panel's main goals were to draw up a code of conduct for public officials, resolutions on bribery and on corruption in international commerce with a view to a possible international treaty, drawing up a "model" law on corruption for countries to adopt on a voluntary basis, and to update a 1992 "practical" U.N. manual on fighting corruption.
